question: A cushion of space around your motorcycle gives you:
choice_a: Time to react and space to maneuver if someone else makes a mistake
choice_b: Better fuel economy
choice_c: A quieter-running engine
choice_d: Protection from weather only
explanation: The best protection you can have is distance -- a cushion of space -- all around your motorcycle, giving you time to react and space to maneuver.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.14, 'Keeping Your Distance'

question: According to the handbook, each traffic lane gives a motorcycle:
choice_a: Only one usable path
choice_b: Three paths of travel
choice_c: Exactly two paths, left and right
choice_d: No usable lane positions
explanation: Each traffic lane gives a motorcycle three paths of travel, as indicated in the handbook's illustration.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.14, 'Lane Positions'

question: Is any portion of the lane, including the center, considered off-limits for lane position?
choice_a: Yes, the center of the lane must always be avoided
choice_b: Yes, only the far-left path may be used
choice_c: No -- no portion of the lane need be avoided, including the center
choice_d: Yes, only the far-right path may be used
explanation: In general, there is no single best position for riders, and no portion of the lane need be avoided -- including the center.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.15, 'Lane Positions'

question: If vehicles or hazards are present on both sides of your lane, the handbook says your best lane position is usually:
choice_a: The far left of the lane
choice_b: The far right of the lane
choice_c: Riding on the shoulder outside the lane
choice_d: The center of the lane, path 2
explanation: If vehicles are being operated on both sides of you, the center of the lane, path 2, is usually your best option.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.15, 'Lane Positions'

question: The oily strip that collects drippings from cars in the center of a lane is usually:
choice_a: No more than about two feet wide, and rarely a traction problem unless the road is wet
choice_b: Wide enough to cover the entire lane
choice_c: More slippery than any other part of the road at all times
choice_d: Found only on gravel roads
explanation: The oily strip in the center portion is usually no more than two feet wide, and unless the road is wet, permits adequate traction to ride on safely.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.15, 'Lane Positions'

question: What minimum following distance behind the vehicle ahead does the handbook recommend?
choice_a: A half-second following distance
choice_b: A two-second following distance
choice_c: A ten-second following distance
choice_d: No minimum following distance is recommended
explanation: Normally, a minimum of two seconds distance should be maintained behind the vehicle ahead.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.15, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: To gauge your following distance, when the rear bumper of the vehicle ahead passes a fixed marker, you should count off:
choice_a: To sixty before proceeding
choice_b: Only to one
choice_c: "One-thousand-one, one-thousand-two"
choice_d: Backwards from ten
explanation: When the rear bumper of the vehicle ahead passes the marker, count off the seconds: "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two."
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.15, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: If the pavement is slippery, you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, or traffic is heavy enough that someone may squeeze in front of you, the handbook recommends opening a following distance of:
choice_a: One second or less
choice_b: Exactly one second
choice_c: No change from the normal following distance
choice_d: Three seconds or more
explanation: A larger cushion of space is needed under these conditions -- open up a three-second or more following distance.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.15-16, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: Why should you keep well behind the vehicle ahead even when you are both stopped?
choice_a: It makes it easier to get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind
choice_b: It is required only in designated school zones
choice_c: It has no safety benefit beyond comfort
choice_d: It prevents the vehicle ahead from seeing your headlight
explanation: Keep well behind the vehicle ahead even when stopped -- this makes it easier to get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.16, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: Riding in the center portion of the lane behind a car tends to put your image:
choice_a: Completely outside the view of all mirrors
choice_b: In the middle of the driver's rearview mirror, where they are most likely to see you
choice_c: Only in the passenger-side mirror
choice_d: Directly in the driver's blind spot
explanation: Riding in the center portion of the lane should put your image in the middle of the rearview mirror -- where a driver is most likely to see you.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.16, 'Following Another Vehicle'

question: According to the handbook, a good way to handle a tailgater is to:
choice_a: Speed up to put distance between you and them
choice_b: Use your horn and make gestures at them
choice_c: Change lanes and let them pass
choice_d: Ignore them and maintain your current speed
explanation: A better way to handle tailgaters is to get them in front of you -- when someone is following too closely, change lanes and let them pass.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.16, 'Being Followed'

question: If you cannot change lanes to let a tailgater pass, the handbook recommends you:
choice_a: Brake suddenly to discourage them
choice_b: Speed up until they can no longer keep up
choice_c: Swerve side to side within the lane
choice_d: Slow down and open extra space ahead of you to give both of you more room and time to react
explanation: If you can't change lanes, slow down and open up extra space ahead of you; this encourages the tailgater to pass and gives both of you more time and space to react.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.16, 'Being Followed'

question: The first step of passing another vehicle, per the handbook, is to:
choice_a: Ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance to increase your line of sight and visibility
choice_b: Immediately move fully into the oncoming lane
choice_c: Accelerate hard from directly behind the vehicle
choice_d: Turn on your high beam and wait
explanation: Ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance to increase your line of sight and make you more visible; signal and check for oncoming traffic.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.17, 'Passing'

question: After moving into the passing lane and accelerating, the handbook says you should ride through the other vehicle's blind spot:
choice_a: As slowly as possible
choice_b: As quickly as possible
choice_c: While looking away from your path of travel
choice_d: Only after signaling twice in a row
explanation: Ride through the blind spot as quickly as possible, then signal again and complete mirror and head checks before returning to your original lane.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.17, 'Passing'

question: When you are being passed by another vehicle, the handbook says you should generally:
choice_a: Move to the far side of the lane away from the passing vehicle
choice_b: Move to the side of the lane closest to the passing vehicle
choice_c: Stay in the center portion of your lane
choice_d: Come to a stop until the vehicle finishes passing
explanation: When you are being passed from behind or by an oncoming vehicle, stay in the center portion of your lane; riding closer to them could be hazardous.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.17, 'Being Passed'

question: Why does the handbook advise against moving to the portion of the lane farthest from a vehicle that is passing you?
choice_a: It increases your motorcycle's fuel consumption
choice_b: It is illegal under North Carolina law
choice_c: It makes your turn signal harder for others to see
choice_d: It might invite the other driver to cut back into your lane too early
explanation: Do not move into the portion of the lane farthest from the passing vehicle -- it might invite the other driver to cut back into your lane too early.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.17, 'Being Passed'

question: Lane sharing -- riding between rows of stopped or moving cars in the same lane -- is described by the handbook as:
choice_a: Usually prohibited and something to discourage
choice_b: Always safe in heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic
choice_c: A recommended technique when running late
choice_d: Only unsafe after dark
explanation: Cars and motorcycles need a full lane to operate safely; lane sharing is usually prohibited and leaves a rider vulnerable to the unexpected.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.18, 'Lane Sharing'

question: To discourage other drivers from sharing your lane, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Ride as far to one edge of the lane as possible at all times
choice_b: Keep a center-portion lane position whenever drivers might be tempted to squeeze by you
choice_c: Stop your motorcycle in the middle of the intersection
choice_d: Speed up whenever traffic becomes heavy
explanation: Discourage lane sharing by others -- keep a center-portion position whenever drivers might be tempted to squeeze by you, such as in heavy traffic or when preparing to turn.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.18, 'Lane Sharing'

question: When a driver on an entrance ramp may not see you on the highway, the handbook advises you to:
choice_a: Speed up to pass them before they merge
choice_b: Flash your high beam and hold your lane position rigidly
choice_c: Give them plenty of room, changing lanes if one is open or adjusting speed if not
choice_d: Move closer to their vehicle to make yourself more visible
explanation: Drivers on an entrance ramp may not see you on the highway; give them plenty of room, change lanes if one is open, or adjust speed to open space for the merging driver.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.18, 'Merging Cars'

question: Why does the handbook advise against riding next to cars or trucks in other lanes when it isn't necessary?
choice_a: It causes excess engine wear over time
choice_b: It is required by law to always ride ahead of or behind other vehicles
choice_c: It has no real safety implication, only a comfort issue
choice_d: You might be in their blind spot, and they can block your escape route if a hazard appears in your own lane
explanation: Do not ride next to cars or trucks if you don't have to -- you might be in their blind spot, and they also block your escape if you come upon danger in your own lane.
source_note: NC DMV Motorcyclists' Handbook (13th Ed., Sept. 2007), p.18, 'Cars Alongside'
